newsitem.title: CROATIA: OSCE judges Croatia election free but not fair.
newsitem.headline: OSCE judges Croatia election free but not fair.

text.p: International election observers said on Monday the Croatian presidential election which President Franjo Tudjman won with 61 percent of the vote was free but not fair.

"Croatia has experienced a free but not fair election. While candidates were able to speak freely, the process leading up to the election was fundamentally flawed," Paul Simon, special coordinator for the election observation mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said in a statement given to reporters.
"(The campaign) did not meet the minimum standards for democracies. By contrast the election itself was -- with some exceptions -- conducted efficiently," Simon's statement said.
Simon is a U.S. senator who was appointed to coordinate the monitoring mission in Croatia. The OSCE established its observation mission a month before the polls to observe the campaign.

Before the vote opposition candidates had already branded the campaign biased and undemocratic because of Tudjman's virtual control of the state media, especially television, and accused him of using his position to promote his candidacy.

Both opposition candidates were subjected to violence during the campaign. One was hit on the head by a Croatian army captain at a rally and the other had stones thrown at his campaign van while touring the country.
